18. Convex Analysis

CNRS & DMA, École Normale Supérieure

Chapter PDF · Complete book

Convexity turns local optimality conditions into certificates of global solutions, even when objectives have corners or encode constraints. This provides a common language for understanding regularization and designing optimization methods. We develop subgradients and normal cones, study convex conjugates and their relation to smoothness, and derive dual problems and optimality conditions.

We write f(x)f(x)f(x) for the objective and xxx for the variable to be optimized. The main references are [13, 4].

18.1 Basics of Convex Analysis¶

We consider minimization problems of the form

min⁡x∈H  f(x)(18.1)\underset{x \in \mathcal{H}}{\min}\; f(x) \tag{18.1}x∈Hmin​f(x)(18.1)

over the finite-dimensional Hilbert space H:=RN\mathcal{H}\mathrel{:=}\mathbb{R}^NH:=RN, with the canonical inner product ⟨⋅, ⋅⟩\langle \cdot,\,\cdot\rangle⟨⋅,⋅⟩.

Many of these results extend to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, with additional hypotheses where compactness is used.

The objective f:H⟶Rˉ:=R∪{+∞}f : \mathcal{H}\longrightarrow \bar{\mathbb{R}}\mathrel{:=}\mathbb{R}\cup \{+\infty\}f:H⟶Rˉ:=R∪{+∞} is convex. Allowing fff to take the value +∞+\infty+∞ encodes constraints directly in the objective; its effective domain is

dom(f):={x  ;  f(x)<+∞}.\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f) \mathrel{:=} \left\{ x \;;\; f(x)<+\infty \right\} .dom(f):={x;f(x)<+∞}.

For a set C⊂H\mathcal{C}\subset \mathcal{H}C⊂H, define the indicator function

ιC(x):={0ifx∈C,+∞otherwise.\iota_{\mathcal{C}}(x) \mathrel{:=} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} 0 \quad \text{if} \quad x \in \mathcal{C}, \\ +\infty \quad\text{otherwise.} \end{array} \right.ιC​(x):={0ifx∈C,+∞otherwise.​

18.1.1 Convex Sets and Functions¶

A set Ω⊂H\Omega\subset \mathcal{H}Ω⊂H is convex if

∀ (x,y,t)∈Ω2×[0,1],(1−t)x+ty∈Ω.\forall \,(x,y,t) \in \Omega^2 \times [0,1], \quad (1-t)x+ty \in \Omega.∀(x,y,t)∈Ω2×[0,1],(1−t)x+ty∈Ω.

A function is convex if

∀ (x,y,t)∈H2×[0,1],f((1−t)x+ty)⩽(1−t)f(x)+tf(y)(18.2)\forall \,(x,y,t) \in \mathcal{H}^2 \times [0,1], \quad f( (1-t)x+ty ) \leqslant(1-t)f(x) + t f(y) \tag{18.2}∀(x,y,t)∈H2×[0,1],f((1−t)x+ty)⩽(1−t)f(x)+tf(y)(18.2)

Equivalently, its epigraph {(x,r)∈H×R  ;  r⩾f(x)}\left\{ (x,r) \in \mathcal{H}\times \mathbb{R} \;;\; r \geqslant f(x) \right\}{(x,r)∈H×R;r⩾f(x)} is convex. The inequality is interpreted in the extended real line Rˉ\bar{\mathbb{R}}Rˉ, with the convention 0⋅(+∞)=00\cdot(+\infty)=00⋅(+∞)=0 at the endpoints t=0,1t=0,1t=0,1.

The function fff is strictly convex if the inequality in (18.2) is strict whenever x,y∈dom(f)x,y\in\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f)x,y∈dom(f) are distinct and 0<t<10<t<10<t<1.

A set Ω\OmegaΩ is convex if and only if ιΩ\iota_{\Omega}ιΩ​ is a convex function.

Figure 18.1. Convexity and strict convexity for functions and sets.

Throughout the chapter, convex functions fff are assumed proper, meaning dom(f)≠∅\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f) \neq \emptysetdom(f)=∅, and lower semicontinuous (lsc), meaning that for every x∈Hx \in \mathcal{H}x∈H,

lim inf⁡y→xf(y)⩾f(x).\liminf_{y \rightarrow x} f(y) \geqslant f(x).y→xliminf​f(y)⩾f(x).

For a convex function, lower semicontinuity is equivalent to the epigraph epi(f)\mathop{\mathrm{epi}}(f)epi(f) being closed.

We denote by Γ0(H)\Gamma_0(\mathcal{H})Γ0​(H) the set of proper convex lsc functions.

18.1.2 First-Order Conditions¶

Existence of minimizers.

We first address existence. Lower semicontinuity and coercivity provide a useful sufficient condition.

Proposition 18.1

If fff is proper, lower semicontinuous, and coercive (i.e. f(x)→+∞f(x)\rightarrow +\inftyf(x)→+∞ as ∣ ⁣∣x∣ ⁣∣→+∞|\!| x |\!|\rightarrow +\infty∣∣x∣∣→+∞), then there exists a minimizer x⋆x^\starx⋆ of fff.

Proof

Choose x0∈dom(f)x_0\in\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f)x0​∈dom(f). The sublevel set K={x:f(x)⩽f(x0)}K=\{x:f(x)\leqslant f(x_0)\}K={x:f(x)⩽f(x0​)} is nonempty, closed by lower semicontinuity, and bounded by coercivity. It is therefore compact in finite dimensions. A lower semicontinuous function attains its infimum on KKK, at some x⋆x^\starx⋆. Since f(x)>f(x0)⩾f(x⋆)f(x)>f(x_0)\geqslant f(x^\star)f(x)>f(x0​)⩾f(x⋆) outside KKK, this point is a global minimizer.

This compactness argument is known as the direct method in the calculus of variations.

For fff in Γ0(H)\Gamma_0(\mathcal{H})Γ0​(H), the minimizer set argminf\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}fargminf is closed and convex, and every local minimizer is global. Strict convexity of fff implies that there is at most one minimizer.

Subdifferential.

The subdifferential at xxx of fff is

∂f(x):={u∈H∗  ;  ∀y∈H,f(y)⩾f(x)+⟨u, y−x⟩},x∈dom(f).\partial f(x) \mathrel{:=} \left\{ u \in \mathcal{H}^* \;;\; \forall y\in\mathcal{H}, f(y) \geqslant f(x) + \langle u,\,y-x\rangle \right\} ,\qquad x\in\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f).∂f(x):={u∈H∗;∀y∈H,f(y)⩾f(x)+⟨u,y−x⟩},x∈dom(f).

We set ∂f(x)=∅\partial f(x)=\emptyset∂f(x)=∅ outside dom(f)\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f)dom(f). Here H∗=RN\mathcal{H}^*=\mathbb{R}^NH∗=RN denotes the space of dual vectors. The inner product identifies the dual space with H\mathcal{H}H, but distinguishing primal and dual variables remains useful. The duality pairing itself is canonical; the identification of a linear functional with a vector depends on the inner product.

The subdifferential ∂f(x)\partial f(x)∂f(x) consists of the slopes uuu of supporting affine functions f(x)+⟨u, z−x⟩f(x) + \langle u,\,z-x\ranglef(x)+⟨u,z−x⟩ that lie below fff.

Figure 18.2. The subdifferential

At an interior point of dom(f)\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f)dom(f), the function fff is differentiable exactly when its subdifferential consists of the gradient alone:

∂f(x)={∇f(x)}.\partial f(x) = \{ \nabla f(x) \}.∂f(x)={∇f(x)}.

Multiple elements of ∂f(x)\partial f(x)∂f(x) indicate distinct supporting slopes of fff at xxx.

The subdifferential can also be empty at a boundary point of the effective domain. For example, f(x)=−1−x2f(x)=-\sqrt{1-x^2}f(x)=−1−x2​ on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], extended by +∞+\infty+∞ outside this interval, has no subgradient at x=±1x=\pm1x=±1.

Since ∂f(x)⊂H∗\partial f(x) \subset \mathcal{H}^*∂f(x)⊂H∗ is an intersection of half-spaces, it is a closed convex set.

Thus ∂f:H↦2H∗\partial f : \mathcal{H}\mapsto 2^{\mathcal{H}^*}∂f:H↦2H∗ is a set-valued operator, also written ∂f:H↪H∗\partial f : \mathcal{H}\hookrightarrow \mathcal{H}^*∂f:H↪H∗.

Remark 18.2 (Maximally monotone operator)

The subdifferential ∂f\partial f∂f is monotone: setting U=∂fU=\partial fU=∂f gives

∀ (u,v)∈U(x)×U(y),⟨y−x, v−u⟩⩾0.\forall \,(u,v) \in U(x) \times U(y), \quad \langle y-x,\,v-u\rangle \geqslant 0.∀(u,v)∈U(x)×U(y),⟨y−x,v−u⟩⩾0.

For single-valued maps on the real line, monotonicity means being nondecreasing.

Subdifferentials can also be shown to be maximally monotone, meaning that their graphs are not properly contained in the graph of another monotone operator.

Conversely, a monotone map need not be a subdifferential; an example is (x,y)↦(−y,x)(x,y) \mapsto (-y,x)(x,y)↦(−y,x).

Many results extend from subdifferentials to arbitrary maximally monotone operators. We restrict attention to subdifferentials here.

For the absolute value f(x)=∣x∣f(x)=|x|f(x)=∣x∣, write ∂f(x)=∂∣⋅∣(x)\partial f(x) = \partial |\cdot|(x)∂f(x)=∂∣⋅∣(x). Its subdifferential is

∂∣⋅∣(x)={{−1}ifx<0,{1}ifx>0,[−1,1]ifx=0.\partial |\cdot|(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \{-1\} \quad \text{if} \quad x < 0, \\ \{1\} \quad \text{if} \quad x > 0, \\ {[-1,1]} \quad \text{if} \quad x=0. \end{array} \right.∂∣⋅∣(x)=⎩⎨⎧​{−1}ifx<0,{1}ifx>0,[−1,1]ifx=0.​

uI=sign(xI)and∣ ⁣∣uIc∣ ⁣∣∞⩽1.u_I = \mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(x_I) \quad \text{and} \quad |\!| u_{I^c} |\!|_\infty \leqslant 1.uI​=sign(xI​)and∣∣uIc​∣∣∞​⩽1.

A sum rule requires a domain qualification. If one function is finite and continuous at a point in the domain of the other, then for every x∈dom(f)∩dom(g)x\in\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f)\cap\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(g)x∈dom(f)∩dom(g),

∂(f+g)(x)=∂f(x)⊕∂g(x)={u+v  ;  (u,v)∈∂f(x)×∂g(x)}\partial (f+g)(x) = \partial f(x) \oplus \partial g(x) = \left\{ u+v \;;\; (u,v) \in \partial f(x) \times \partial g(x) \right\}∂(f+g)(x)=∂f(x)⊕∂g(x)={u+v;(u,v)∈∂f(x)×∂g(x)}

where ⊕\oplus⊕ denotes the Minkowski sum. In particular, if fff is differentiable at xxx, then

∂(f+g)(x)=∇f(x)+∂g(x)={∇f(x)+v  ;  v∈∂g(x)}.\partial (f+g)(x) = \nabla f(x) + \partial g(x) = \left\{ \nabla f(x) + v \;;\; v \in \partial g(x) \right\} .∂(f+g)(x)=∇f(x)+∂g(x)={∇f(x)+v;v∈∂g(x)}.

Positive scaling gives

∀ λ>0,∂(λf)(x)=λ(∂f(x)).\forall \,\lambda>0, \quad \partial (\lambda f)(x) = \lambda(\partial f(x)).∀λ>0,∂(λf)(x)=λ(∂f(x)).

Composition with a linear map does preserve convexity. ∀ x∈C,∂ιC(x)=NC(x):={v  ;  ∀ z∈C,⟨z−x, v⟩⩽0}.\forall \,x \in \mathcal{C}, \quad \partial \iota_\mathcal{C}(x) = \mathcal{N}_\mathcal{C}(x) \mathrel{:=} \left\{ v \;;\; \forall \,z \in \mathcal{C}, \langle z-x,\,v\rangle \leqslant 0 \right\} .∀x∈C,∂ιC​(x)=NC​(x):={v;∀z∈C,⟨z−x,v⟩⩽0}.

Outside the set, x∉Cx \notin \mathcal{C}x∈/C implies ∂ιC(x)=∅\partial \iota_\mathcal{C}(x) = \emptyset∂ιC​(x)=∅.

For an affine space C=a+V\mathcal{C}= a+\mathcal{V}C=a+V with direction space V⊂H\mathcal{V}\subset \mathcal{H}V⊂H, the normal cone at each of its points is NC(x)=V⊥\mathcal{N}_\mathcal{C}(x)=\mathcal{V}^\botNC​(x)=V⊥, the orthogonal complement of V\mathcal{V}V. 18.2 Legendre–Fenchel Transform¶

The Legendre–Fenchel transform provides a dual representation of a convex function. It makes many Lagrange-duality calculations systematic by expressing inner minimizations through conjugates.

18.2.1 Legendre Transform¶

For f∈Γ0(H)f \in \Gamma_0(\mathcal{H})f∈Γ0​(H), we define its Legendre–Fenchel transform, or convex conjugate, by

f∗(u):=sup⁡x  ⟨x, u⟩−f(x).(18.3)f^*(u) \mathrel{:=}\underset{x}{\sup}\; \langle x,\,u\rangle - f(x). \tag{18.3}f∗(u):=xsup​⟨x,u⟩−f(x).(18.3)

As a supremum of continuous affine functions, f∗f^*f∗ is convex and lower semicontinuous; in fact, f⋆∈Γ0(H∗)f^\star \in \Gamma_0(\mathcal{H}^*)f⋆∈Γ0​(H∗). The following biconjugacy theorem recovers the original function.

Theorem 18.5

One has

∀ f∈Γ0(H),(f∗)∗=f.\forall \,f \in \Gamma_0(\mathcal{H}), \quad (f^{*})^* = f.∀f∈Γ0​(H),(f∗)∗=f.

Even when fff is not convex, f∗f^*f∗ is convex. If fff admits an affine minorant, f∗∗f^{**}f∗∗ is its lower semicontinuous convex envelope: the largest lower semicontinuous convex function below fff.

The subdifferentials of fff and f∗f^*f∗ satisfy the following inverse relation.

Proposition 18.6

We have ∂f∗=(∂f)−1\partial f^* = (\partial f)^{-1}∂f∗=(∂f)−1, where the inverse of a set-valued map is defined in (19.15). The Fenchel–Young inequality states that

∀ (x,y),⟨x, y⟩⩽f(x)+f∗(y).\forall \,(x,y), \quad \langle x,\,y\rangle \leqslant f(x) + f^*(y).∀(x,y),⟨x,y⟩⩽f(x)+f∗(y).

Equality is characterized by

⟨x, y⟩=f(x)+f∗(y)⇔x∈∂f∗(y)⇔y∈∂f(x).\langle x,\,y\rangle = f(x) + f^*(y) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x \in \partial f^*(y) \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad y \in \partial f(x).⟨x,y⟩=f(x)+f∗(y)⇔x∈∂f∗(y)⇔y∈∂f(x).
Proposition 18.7

For 1⩽p,q⩽∞1\leqslant p,q\leqslant\infty1⩽p,q⩽∞ with 1/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=1,

(ι∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣p⩽1)∗=∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣qand(∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣q)∗=ι∣ ⁣∣⋅∣ ⁣∣p⩽1( \iota_{|\!| \cdot |\!|_p \leqslant 1} )^* = |\!| \cdot |\!|_q \quad \text{and} \quad ( |\!| \cdot |\!|_q )^* = \iota_{|\!| \cdot |\!|_p \leqslant 1}(ι∣∣⋅∣∣p​⩽1​)∗=∣∣⋅∣∣q​and(∣∣⋅∣∣q​)∗=ι∣∣⋅∣∣p​⩽1​

18.2.2 Legendre Transform and Smoothness¶

The Legendre–Fenchel transform exchanges smoothness and strong convexity. It inverts subdifferentials; when fff is twice continuously differentiable with positive definite Hessian and y=∇f(x)y=\nabla f(x)y=∇f(x), the inverse function theorem yields

∂2f∗(y)=(∂2f(x))−1.\partial^2 f^*(y)=(\partial^2 f(x))^{-1}.∂2f∗(y)=(∂2f(x))−1.

The next statement gives a version of this correspondence that does not require second derivatives.

Proposition 18.9

For f∈Γ0(H)f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal{H})f∈Γ0​(H) and L>0L>0L>0,

18.3 Convex Duality¶

A dual problem depends on the chosen primal formulation. A change of variables or a different representation of the constraints can produce a different dual problem.

18.3.1 Lagrange Duality: Affine Constraints¶

Begin with affine equality constraints:

min⁡Ax=y  f(x)\underset{Ax=y}{\min}\; f(x)Ax=ymin​f(x)

where A∈RP×pA\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times p}A∈RP×p, y∈RPy\in\mathbb{R}^Py∈RP, and f:Rp→Rf : \mathbb{R}^p \rightarrow \mathbb{R}f:Rp→R is convex and finite everywhere, hence continuous.

Assume that the affine constraint is feasible. Introducing u∈RPu\in\mathbb{R}^Pu∈RP gives the Lagrangian L(x,u)=f(x)+⟨Ax−y, u⟩\mathcal{L}(x,u)=f(x)+\langle Ax-y,\,u\rangleL(x,u)=f(x)+⟨Ax−y,u⟩. Minimization over xxx yields

F(u)=−f∗(−A∗u)−⟨y, u⟩.F(u)=-f^*(-A^*u)-\langle y,\,u\rangle.F(u)=−f∗(−A∗u)−⟨y,u⟩.

Because fff is finite and continuous everywhere, feasibility is a sufficient qualification for strong duality:

inf⁡Ax=y  f(x)=sup⁡u∈RP  {−f∗(−A∗u)−⟨y, u⟩}.\underset{Ax=y}{\inf}\;f(x)=\underset{u\in\mathbb{R}^P}{\sup}\;\{-f^*(-A^*u)-\langle y,\,u\rangle\}.Ax=yinf​f(x)=u∈RPsup​{−f∗(−A∗u)−⟨y,u⟩}.

A primal-dual optimal pair satisfies Ax⋆=yAx^\star=yAx⋆=y and −A∗u⋆∈∂f(x⋆)-A^*u^\star\in\partial f(x^\star)−A∗u⋆∈∂f(x⋆).

18.3.2 Lagrange Duality: General Case¶

We consider a minimization of the form

p⋆=inf⁡x∈RN  {f(x)  ;  Ax=yandg(x)⩽0}(18.5)p^\star = \underset{x \in \mathbb{R}^N}{\inf}\; \left\{ f(x) \;;\; Ax=y \quad \text{and} \quad g(x) \leqslant 0 \right\} \tag{18.5}p⋆=x∈RNinf​{f(x);Ax=yandg(x)⩽0}(18.5)

for a continuous convex function f:H→Rf : \mathcal{H}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}f:H→R, a matrix A∈RP×NA \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times N}A∈RP×N and a function g:H→RQg : \mathcal{H}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^Qg:H→RQ such that each coordinate gi:H→Rg_i : \mathcal{H}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}gi​:H→R is continuous and convex.

In the standard formulation of a convex program, equality constraints are affine.

Problems with convex inequality constraints can be written in the form (18.5). The representation is not unique, and different formulations lead to different dual problems.

For simplicity, fff is assumed finite and continuous on its full domain dom(f)=RN\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f)=\mathbb{R}^Ndom(f)=RN.

The theory extends to more general dom(f)\mathop{\mathrm{dom}}(f)dom(f), with additional domain qualifications. Here all constraints are expressed through Ax=yAx=yAx=y and g(x)⩽0g(x) \leqslant 0g(x)⩽0.

Conic duality extends this construction from nonnegativity x⩾0x \geqslant 0x⩾0 to positive semidefiniteness X⪰0X \succeq 0X⪰0 of a matrix XXX, and more generally to membership in a convex cone.

We use the following fact

Define the Lagrangian by

L(x,u,v):=f(x)+⟨Ax−y, u⟩+⟨g(x), v⟩.\mathcal{L}(x,u,v) \mathrel{:=}f(x) + \langle Ax-y,\,u\rangle + \langle g(x),\,v\rangle.L(x,u,v):=f(x)+⟨Ax−y,u⟩+⟨g(x),v⟩.

The dual objective FFF is concave because it is an infimum of affine functions. The dual problem therefore maximizes a concave objective.

Weak duality states that every feasible dual value is a lower bound on the primal optimum.

18.3.3 Fenchel–Rockafellar Duality¶

Conjugates often give explicit expressions for the Lagrange dual of an objective fff. Fenchel–Rockafellar duality is a particularly useful example.

We consider the following structured minimization problem

p⋆=inf⁡x  f(x)+g(Ax).(18.12)p^\star = \underset{x}{\inf}\; f(x) + g(Ax). \tag{18.12}p⋆=xinf​f(x)+g(Ax).(18.12)

Introducing an auxiliary variable gives

inf⁡y=Ax  f(x)+g(y).\underset{y=Ax}{\inf}\; f(x) + g(y).y=Axinf​f(x)+g(y).

We can then form the primal-dual problem

inf⁡(x,y)  sup⁡u  f(x)+g(y)+⟨Ax−y, u⟩.(18.13)\underset{(x,y)}{\inf}\; \underset{u}{\sup}\; f(x) + g(y) + \langle Ax-y,\,u\rangle. \tag{18.13}(x,y)inf​usup​f(x)+g(y)+⟨Ax−y,u⟩.(18.13)

Under the domain qualification in Theorem 18.12, one can exchange the infimum and supremum to obtain the dual problem

=sup⁡u  {(inf⁡x  ⟨x, A∗u⟩+f(x))+(inf⁡y  −⟨y, u⟩+g(y))}.(18.15)\begin{aligned} &= \underset{u}{\sup}\; \left\{\left( \underset{x}{\inf}\; \langle x,\,A^* u\rangle + f(x) \right) + \left( \underset{y}{\inf}\; -\langle y,\,u\rangle + g(y) \right)\right\}. \end{aligned} \tag{18.15}​=usup​{(xinf​⟨x,A∗u⟩+f(x))+(yinf​−⟨y,u⟩+g(y))}.​(18.15)
